title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
gist: Ai2 interviewed 17 US-based scientists about agentic AI for research and found trust rests on five dimensions (validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, transparency) beyond answer correctness. Ai2 argues scientists should shape which tasks agents take, how they operate, and how they are benchmarked, pointing toward a participatory benchmark and features like transparent action logs and granular data controls.

insights.claim: Ai2's interviews with 17 scientists identified five dimensions of scientific trust in AI agents: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency — concerns that go beyond whether the AI produces a correct answer.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Agentic research tools will be judged on auditability and data governance, not just accuracy — a product-requirement signal for AI-for-science vendors.
insights.quote: we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency
insights.locator: One of our main findings concerns trust

insights.claim: A technically correct result from an AI agent may still be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced or if the agent accessed confidential data or files beyond what was authorized.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Provenance/trace logging and access scoping become table-stakes features for scientific agent platforms.

insights.claim: Ai2 notes that much existing safety work on scientific AI applications focuses on catastrophic risks in biology and nuclear physics, while evaluation of whether agents follow everyday responsible-conduct-of-research standards is underdeveloped.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Gap in the eval market: field-specific research-conduct benchmarks rather than only catastrophic-risk evals.
insights.quote: much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics
insights.locator: Our interest in these questions grew

insights.claim: Scientists reported checking AI-generated answers against original publications, worrying about confident responses with subtle inaccuracies and retrieval tools that surface only studies supporting a favored hypothesis.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Confirmation-bias in retrieval is a named failure mode; tools that surface contradictory evidence could differentiate.
insights.locator: Several participants described checking AI-generated answers

insights.claim: Ai2 proposes agent benchmarks that test research conduct, e.g. whether a literature-review agent overlooks contradictory evidence, whether a coding agent accesses files outside its authorized scope, and whether data-processing agents' methods match established human workflows.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Watch for new process-level scientific agent benchmarks from Ai2 that could become procurement criteria.
insights.locator: Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents

insights.claim: Ai2's longer-term goal is a participatory benchmark in which scientists define the research practices and safety requirements agents are tested against, applied to systems from Ai2 or elsewhere; these remain proposals, not established solutions.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Early signal of a community-defined eval standard that could rate third-party scientific agents.
insights.quote: a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against
insights.locator: These examples point toward a longer-term goal

insights.claim: Some scientists fear AI-assisted research diminishes learning; an early-career biologist deliberately limited AI use while acquiring skills, and the value of automation depends on whether the researcher already masters the task.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Adoption of research agents may be slower among trainees and in teaching settings, shaping enterprise/academic seat growth.
insights.locator: An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use

insights.claim: A political scientist who used Claude to revise a manuscript then rewrote the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Authorship ambiguity is a real friction for AI writing tools in academia; attribution/tracking features may matter.
insights.quote: I don’t know what was AI and what was me
insights.locator: Even researchers who tried AI for writing

insights.claim: Scientists draw different lines: one biologist refused to use AI for generating research ideas, while an anthropologist argued routine methods and results sections are formulaic enough to automate.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Writing automation of formulaic paper sections is the lower-resistance wedge versus ideation.

insights.claim: Using AI to critique one's own manuscript was viewed favorably, but using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns over confidentiality, attribution and fair evaluation in peer review.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: AI peer-review tooling faces norm-based resistance distinct from capability limits.

insights.claim: Because fields and individuals differ, responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Configurable, field-specific policy controls beat one-size-fits-all guardrails in scientific AI products.
insights.quote: responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks
insights.locator: These disagreements suggest that responsible automation

insights.claim: Content restrictions that stop AI tools from discussing certain topics can interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations, while researchers with human-subject data want stronger privacy and access guarantees.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Overly broad model refusals are a product liability for research users; tunable safeguards are a competitive axis.
insights.locator: The same tension applies to safeguards

insights.claim: Ai2 argues scientific communities need a meaningful role in setting AI assistance boundaries, so developers learn which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards might obstruct valuable work.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Co-design with domain users is Ai2's positioning for open scientific tools.
insights.locator: This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role

themes.theme: Ai2's design priorities and study limits

insights.claim: Ai2 says trustworthy scientific agents will require transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, plus evaluations informed by each scientific community's standards.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Action-audit trails and fine-grained data permissions are likely feature priorities in Ai2's scientific agent work.
insights.quote: transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls
insights.locator: Researchers should be able to examine

insights.claim: The study is exploratory: interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Treat findings as qualitative design signals, not market-sizing evidence.
insights.locator: It will also require continued collaboration.

insights.claim: Interviewees were split between excitement about AI-driven scientific progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists, and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.
insights.speaker: Kyle Wiggers
insights.so_what: Institutional AI-use guidelines and training are an emerging need in research institutions.
insights.locator: A third key finding pertains to the future of science
